opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one of the most exciting parts of working on something like Genie 3. When you build a model that can generate interactive, explorable worlds in real time from a text prompt, you don't fully know in advance what people will do with it. So a big part of our approach has been to stay open and treat discovery as part of the research itself.

A few directions felt natural from the start. One is training embodied agents. If you want agents that can act in the world, you need lots of rich, diverse environments, and building those by hand is slow and expensive. A world model that can generate an effectively unlimited variety of consistent environments, where an agent can move around and take actions, is a powerful tool there. We've already seen that it's useful to put agents into these generated worlds and give them goals.

Then there's the creative side: education, storytelling, prototyping experiences, letting someone step into a place that's hard or impossible to visit, whether that's a historical setting or just something imaginative. But I try to be careful not to over-index on any one use case, because the history of these technologies shows that the most interesting applications often come from people outside the research team.

That's why we've been rolling it out gradually, getting it into the hands of a small group of researchers and creators, watching how they use it, and learning where it shines and where it breaks. The model still has real limitations: interactions can only last so long, the range of actions an agent can take is limited, and things like accurate text rendering or modeling multiple agents interacting are still hard. Seeing where people hit those walls tells us both what to improve and what applications are realistic today versus a year or two from now.

So it's a mix of strong intuitions, like agent training and interactive media, and a deliberate humility about what we don't know yet. Some of the best ideas will probably come from someone playing with it and saying, "wait, what if I tried this?"

r001.rationale: The response says the model is being tried by a small group of researchers and creators, whose use helps reveal where it works and what applications are realistic. It does not identify them as trusted testers or academics, or clearly describe their feedback as the method for discovering promising applications.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one we're still figuring out ourselves. I think the honest answer is that when you build something like Genie 3, you have some hypotheses going in, but a lot of the interesting applications emerge from just putting it in front of people and watching what they do with it.

So the way I think about it, there are a few buckets. The first one, and the one that's closest to why we built it, is as a training environment for embodied agents. If you want agents that can act in the world, they need a lot of experience, and the real world is slow and expensive and sometimes dangerous. Having a model that can generate an unbounded variety of interactive worlds, where you can set up a scenario, have an agent act in it, and see the consequences unfold in real time, that's potentially a huge deal for robotics and for agent research more broadly. So that's the application we had in mind from the start.

The second bucket is more about people. Things like education, where you could drop a student into a world and let them explore it, or creative tools, prototyping, game design, where someone can sketch an idea and immediately be walking around in it. And what's been striking to us is how different that feels from a video model. The moment you can control it, the moment it responds to you, people engage with it in a completely different way.

And then there's a third bucket, which is the stuff we haven't thought of. Every time we show it to a new group, somebody comes up with something that surprises us. So we try to stay fairly humble about it. We're not trying to lock down use cases too early. We'd rather get it into the hands of researchers and creators, see what resonates, and let that feed back into where we push the research next.

I'd also say we're deliberately treating this as a research preview rather than a product, because the model still has real limitations. The action space is limited, memory over long horizons is still something we're working on, and interactions between multiple agents are hard. So part of discovering applications is also discovering where it breaks, and that tells us a lot about what to build next.

r001.rationale: The response recommends showing Genie 3 to researchers, creators, and other groups, but does not specifically present feedback from trusted testers or academics as the discovery method.

astra-6.text:
I think at this stage, we’re still discovering what this kind of model is useful for. You can have ideas about applications, but when you can actually interact with a world and try things, you start to see possibilities—and limitations—that weren’t obvious beforehand.

So I think the process is to put it in front of people with different perspectives, see what they try to do, and learn from that. Some people might approach it as a creative tool; others might be interested in environments where an agent can practice and learn. Those lead to different questions about what the model needs to do well.

The important thing is to stay open, while distinguishing something that makes a compelling demonstration from something that reliably solves a problem for someone. We’re early in that process.

r001.rationale: The response says to put the model in front of people with different perspectives and learn from what they try, but it does not identify them as trusted testers or academics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think at this stage, a lot of it is about putting the model in people’s hands and seeing what they discover. We have intuitions about applications—interactive experiences, creative tools, environments for training agents—but those intuitions are shaped by how we’ve been working with it internally.

When you can create a world and interact with it, people start asking questions that they wouldn’t ask of a video model. Can I explore this place? Can I try a different action and see what happens? That opens up a different set of possibilities.

So I think the process is exploratory: work with people who have different needs, understand where the model is useful today, and learn where its limitations get in the way. That feedback helps us figure out both the applications and what capabilities to develop next.

r001.rationale: The response says to work with people with different needs and use their feedback to identify applications, but it does not specify trusted testers or academics.
